summary: Collects implementation reports from vendors, consortiums and researchers who built systems using standards from the IETF INCH and MILE working groups on sharing security incident information. It shows which of those standards are actually in use.

plainLanguage.summary: A club asks each member which of its games they actually play. This document is the list of answers from people who tried the incident-sharing standards.

questions: how do security teams share incident information
subtitle: A survey of how the incident-sharing standards from IETF are actually being implemented

tldr.problem: The IETF working groups INCH and MILE defined protocols for sharing security incident information between organizations, but it was unclear how many implementers had adopted these standards or how they were being used in practice.
tldr.mechanism: This document collects implementation reports from vendors, consortiums, researchers, and open source projects that have built systems based on IODEF and related incident-sharing standards. It documents real deployments in ISACs, CSIRTs, and security operations centers.
tldr.outcome: The reports show that IODEF and related MILE standards are deployed in diverse implementations ranging from open source libraries to commercial security platforms, and identifies common implementation challenges such as XML schema complexity.

facts.label: Implementation categories
facts.value: Consortiums, open source, vendor products, planned systems, research systems

today: RFC 8134 is an Informational document published in May 2017. It provides a snapshot of IODEF implementations at that time. IODEF remains the standard format for incident information exchange, used by national security organizations, ISACs, and incident response teams. The challenges documented regarding XML schema complexity remain relevant for new implementers.

sections.title: Standards for Sharing Incident Information
sections.content:
Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs) and information sharing organizations need to exchange details about security incidents: what systems were affected, what happened, what impact occurred, and what response actions were taken. The IETF working groups INCH (Incident Handling) and MILE (Management Incident Lightweight Exchange) published standards to define how this information should be formatted and exchanged.

The standards include IODEF (Incident Object Description Exchange Format), which provides a framework for encoding incident data in a structured XML format. IODEF is used alongside transport protocols like RID (Real-time Inter-network Defense) and extensions for specific incident types such as phishing and fraud.

This document collects reports from vendors, research teams, consortiums, and open source projects showing which standards they have implemented and how they use them in practice. The reports document real deployments including national information sharing organizations, commercial security products, and research prototypes.
sections.plainLanguage: When a cyber attack happens, security teams need to tell each other "We were hit, here's what we know, please help." IETF made a language (IODEF) so everyone can understand the messages. This document shows who actually uses it.

sections.title: Implementation Categories
sections.content:
The RFC documents implementations across several categories:

Consortiums and ISACs: The Anti-Phishing Working Group (APWG), Advanced Cyber Defence Centre (ACDC), and Research and Education Networking Information Sharing and Analysis Center (REN-ISAC) have integrated IODEF into their threat-sharing platforms. These organizations represent hundreds of members exchanging incident and threat data.

Open Source Projects: Multiple open source implementations exist, including the EMC/RSA RID Agent (implementing RID and IODEF), NICT's IODEF-SCI tools for embedding structured cyber security information, and n6, a platform for processing security data with REST APIs and support for IODEF and other formats.

Vendor Products: Deep Secure provides guards for protecting IODEF/RID exchanges over HTTPS and XMPP. DFLabs IncMan Suite implements IODEF import/export for incident management. Surevine developed a proof of concept using XMPP extensions for IODEF. The MANTIS framework demonstrates how STIX, CybOX, and IODEF can be managed together.

Planned Implementations: HP Threat Central and NICT's DAEDALUS have announced plans to support IODEF in future versions, with HP integrating IODEF into their ArcSight SIEM platform.
sections.plainLanguage: Big organizations like anti-phishing groups use it, programmers made open source versions, companies built products with it, and some companies plan to add it soon.

sections.title: Standards Being Implemented
sections.content:
The implementations cover multiple IETF standards published from INCH and MILE:

RFC 5070 (IODEF v1) is the original Incident Object Description Exchange Format specification. Implementations encode incident details as XML describing affected systems, timelines, impacts, and technical indicators.

RFC 7970 (IODEF v2) is the updated version with enhancements for modern incident data.

RFC 5901 extends IODEF specifically for reporting phishing incidents, used by the APWG.

RFC 5941 defines how to share transaction fraud data in IODEF format.

RFC 6545 (RID) defines the Real-time Inter-network Defense protocol for automated incident response coordination between networks. RFC 6546 specifies how to transport RID messages over HTTP/TLS.

RFC 7203 (IODEF-SCI) extends IODEF to embed Structured Cybersecurity Information, allowing IODEF documents to contain Malware Metadata (MMDEF), Common Event Expression (CEE), and malware analysis (MAEC) data alongside incident descriptions.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different versions of the format (old and new), special versions for phishing and fraud, a protocol for fast responses (RID), and an extension for adding detailed technical data about malware and threats.

sections.title: Real-World Deployments
sections.content:
The implementations show diverse use cases. The Collaborative Incident Management System (CIMS) used IODEF with Request Tracker (RT) to allow teams working in the NATO Cyber Coalition exercise to operate separate incident tickets while collaborating through IODEF messages in email. When any team modified an incident, an IODEF message was generated and sent to other participating CSIRTs.

AirCERT, built by CERT/CC, is a distributed system for collecting flow data and Intrusion Detection System alerts into a database and sharing them using IODEF and the Intrusion Detection Message Exchange Format (IDMEF). It was designed for large-scale deployment with the ability to sanitize data before sharing across trust boundaries.

The US Department of Energy's CyberFed system automates the collection of network alerts from firewalls, IDS/IPS systems, and proxies and converts them to IODEF-formatted blocking indicators that are deployed machine-to-machine across the network. CyberFed supports multiple formats including IODEF and STIX.

These deployments demonstrate that IODEF is used not just for incident description but for automating incident response, coordination between teams, and distribution of defensive indicators.
sections.plainLanguage: In real use, teams send IODEF messages over email when incidents change, computers collect alerts and automatically tell other computers to block attacks, and national security labs share threat information in IODEF format.

sections.title: Implementation Challenges and Tools
sections.content:
The RFC documents practical challenges encountered by implementers. The IODEF XML schema is complex, and several code generators for XML bindings (such as JAXB for Java and Ruby's RXSD) failed to properly process it. Only PyXB (Python), CodeSynthesis XSD (C++), and Xsd.exe (C#) successfully generated code from the schema. A workaround is double-conversion of the XSD: serializing it to XML and converting back to XSD.

The IODEF schema uses hyphens in class names (like "IODEF-Document" and "vlan-name") and extension attributes (like "ext-value"). Many programming languages prohibit hyphens in identifiers, so code generators must replace them, then restore them when outputting XML.

To address complexity, multiple libraries were developed. iodeflib is a Python library providing a simpler interface than auto-generated bindings, hiding unnecessary nesting and offering convenient shortcuts. iodefpm is a Perl module for parsing key-value formats into IODEF and includes a generic XML parser.

The RFC also provides usability tips, such as randomizing incident ID assignment to prevent information leakage about incident volumes, and carefully choosing category attributes when describing systems that serve multiple roles.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing code to handle IODEF's complex format is hard; most automatic code generators choke on it. Smart programmers made easier libraries, and there are tricks like randomizing ID numbers to keep information secret.
